summary: Recursion solves a problem by having a function call itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function needs a base case that stops the calls and a recursive case that makes progress toward it.

sections.heading: Anatomy
bullets: Base case: the smallest input, answered directly.
Recursive case: reduce the problem and combine the sub-result.
Progress: each call must move closer to the base case or recursion never ends.

sections.heading: The call stack
sections.body: Each call pushes a stack frame holding its parameters, locals, and return address. Calls wait in LIFO order, and results return as frames pop. fact(4) pushes fact(4), fact(3), fact(2), fact(1), then unwinds multiplying 1, 2, 6, 24. Depth n uses O(n) stack, and missing or unreachable base cases overflow it.

sections.heading: Classic examples
bullets: Factorial and sum of 1..n: linear recursion.
Fibonacci: tree recursion, exponential time when naive.
Power by squaring: halve the exponent each call, O(log n).
Tower of Hanoi: move n-1 disks, move one, move n-1 again; 2^n - 1 moves.
Binary search, merge sort, quick sort, tree traversals.

sections.heading: Recursion versus iteration
bullets: Recursion mirrors recursive structures (trees, divide and conquer) and is often shorter.
Iteration avoids stack growth and call overhead.
Any recursion can be rewritten with an explicit stack.
Deep recursion in C risks stack overflow (typically a few hundred thousand frames).

sections.heading: Analyzing cost
sections.body: Write a recurrence and solve it. Factorial: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1) = O(n). Binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n). Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n). Naive Fibonacci: T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) = O(2^n), because it recomputes subproblems.

subtopics.title: Tail recursion
subtopics.summary: Recursive call is the last action.

sections.body: If the call is in tail position, the frame can be reused, making it as cheap as a loop. Scheme guarantees this; C compilers often do it at -O2 but the standard does not require it.
sections.code: long fact_tail(int n, long acc) { return n <= 1 ? acc : fact_tail(n - 1, acc * n); }

sections.body: Build a solution step by step, recurse, and undo the step if it leads nowhere. Used for permutations, subsets, N-Queens, Sudoku, and maze solving. Pruning invalid partial solutions keeps it practical.
Store each computed result by argument so repeated subproblems return instantly. This turns naive Fibonacci from O(2^n) into O(n) and is the top-down form of dynamic programming.
isEven(n) calls isOdd(n-1) and vice versa. Declare prototypes first. Recursive-descent parsers use this heavily, one function per grammar rule.

bullets: Verify the base case first, including empty input.
Print depth and arguments to trace calls.
Check that each call strictly reduces the problem.

takeaways: Base case plus a recursive step that makes progress.
Each call uses a stack frame: depth equals memory.
Naive tree recursion can be exponential; memoize to fix it.
Tail calls and explicit stacks avoid overflow.
